title: Waves, Half-Life and Density
description: v=fλ, exponential half-life reasoning and ρ=m/V.

method_card.title: Waves, Half-Life and Density
method_card.content:
Three distinct recall equations from different areas of physics — all appear every year and are straightforward once the equations are secure.

Recall equations:

  • \(v = f\lambda\) — wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
  • \(\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}\) — density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) ÷ volume (m³)

Half-life (exponential decay — no single formula needed for GCSE): After each half-life, the count rate (or number of undecayed nuclei) halves. Strategy: count how many half-lives fit in the given time, then halve repeatedly. For multi-step questions, construct a table:

Number of half-livesActivity remaining
0Initial
1½ of initial
2¼ of initial
3⅛ of initial

Unit checks:
Wave equation: wavelength in metres, frequency in Hz (= per second), speed in m/s. Density: mass in kg, volume in m³ (note: 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³).
steps: Wave equation: identify two of {v, f, λ} and solve for the third using v = fλ
Density: identify two of {ρ, m, V} and solve for the third using ρ = m ÷ V
Half-life: find n = total time ÷ half-life period, then halve the initial activity n times
For density problems, check unit consistency — convert cm³ to m³ if needed (÷ 1 000 000)
State the answer with the correct unit every time

exam_context.marks: 2–4 marks per calculation; half-life may be paired with graph reading or context questions
exam_context.frequency: High — all three equation types appear regularly; half-life calculation is almost annual

worked_examples.question: A sound wave has a frequency of 400 Hz and a wavelength of 0.85 m. Calculate the wave speed.
A radioactive source has an initial activity of 6400 Bq. Its half-life is 2 hours. Calculate the activity after 8 hours.
A block of aluminium has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate the density in kg/m³.

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 6.8 m. Calculate the wave speed.

misconceptions.message: v = f × λ = 50 × 6.8 = 340 m/s. Don't add frequency and wavelength.

bronze.display: A wave travels at 300 000 000 m/s with a wavelength of 0.10 m. Calculate the frequency.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ = 3×10⁸ ÷ 0.10 = 3×10⁹ Hz. Don't divide λ by v.

bronze.display: An object has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 250 cm³. Calculate the density in g/cm³.
bronze.equation_hint: \(\rho = m \div V\) — units match (g and cm³), so answer is in g/cm³.

misconceptions.message: ρ = 500 ÷ 250 = 2.0 g/cm³. Don't divide volume by mass.

bronze.display: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 800 Bq. After one half-life, what is the count rate?
bronze.equation_hint: After one half-life, the activity halves.

misconceptions.message: After one half-life the count rate is halved: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 Bq.

bronze.display: A source has an activity of 320 Bq. Its half-life is 5 years. What is the activity after 15 years?
bronze.equation_hint: How many half-lives in 15 years? Then halve that many times.

bronze.display: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz (1×10⁸ Hz) and travels at 3×10⁸ m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
A block of iron has mass 7.8 kg and volume 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the density in kg/m³.
A source has an initial count rate of 3200 Bq and a half-life of 10 minutes. What is the count rate after 40 minutes?

silver.display: The activity of a radioactive isotope falls from 1000 Bq to 125 Bq in 30 days. Calculate the half-life.
silver.equation_hint: How many times do you have to halve 1000 to reach 125? Then divide total time by that number.

misconceptions.message: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125: that is 3 halvings. Half-life = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 days.
Count halvings: 1000÷2=500, ÷2=250, ÷2=125 — 3 half-lives. Half-life = 30÷3 = 10 days.

silver.display: An ultrasound pulse travels at 1500 m/s in soft tissue. The pulse has a wavelength of 0.15 mm. Calculate the frequency in Hz. (1 mm = 0.001 m)
silver.equation_hint: Convert wavelength to metres first, then \(f = v \div \lambda\)

silver.display: A wooden block of density 0.80 g/cm³ has a volume of 500 cm³. Calculate its mass in grams.

misconceptions.message: m = ρ × V = 0.80 × 500 = 400 g. Units match (g/cm³ × cm³ = g).

silver.display: A sample of carbon-14 has a half-life of approximately 5700 years. A fossil bone has 25% of the original carbon-14 activity. Estimate the age of the fossil.

misconceptions.message: 25% = ¼ of original. 100% → 50% (1 half-life) → 25% (2 half-lives). Age = 2 × 5700 = 11400 years.
Halving twice gives ¼ of original. 2 half-lives × 5700 years = 11400 years.

silver.display: A stone has a mass of 1.62 kg. When placed in a measuring cylinder it displaces 600 cm³ of water. Calculate the density of the stone in kg/m³.
silver.equation_hint: Convert cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), then \(\rho = m \div V\)

misconceptions.message: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. Multiply cm³ by 10⁻⁶ to convert to m³.

silver.display: A seismic P-wave travels at 6000 m/s through rock. If it has a frequency of 0.5 Hz, calculate its wavelength.

misconceptions.message: λ = v ÷ f = 6000 ÷ 0.5 = 12000 m (12 km). Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a larger result.

gold.display: A radioactive source has an activity of 5400 Bq. After 60 minutes its activity is 675 Bq. Calculate the half-life in minutes.

misconceptions.message: 5400 → 2700 → 1350 → 675: 3 halvings. Half-life = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes.
Count halvings from 5400 to 675: divide by 2 three times. 60 min ÷ 3 = 20 min.

gold.display: An ocean wave has a speed of 15 m/s and a period of 8.0 s. Calculate (a) the frequency and (b) the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: First convert period to frequency: f = 1/T = 0.125 Hz. Then λ = v/f = 15/0.125 = 120 m.

gold.display: A hollow steel ball has an outer volume of 120 cm³ and a mass of 250 g. Calculate the density of the steel ball in g/cm³ and explain why this is less than the density of solid steel (≈7.8 g/cm³).
options: 2.1 g/cm³ — less than solid steel because part of the volume is air, not steel
7.8 g/cm³ — the density is the same because the material is the same
2.1 g/cm³ — less than solid steel because the ball is cooler
0.48 g/cm³ — calculated using total volume without accounting for the shell

misconceptions.message: ρ = 250÷120 = 2.08 g/cm³ ≈ 2.1 g/cm³. This is less than solid steel (7.8) because the total volume includes the hollow air space, not just steel.

gold.display: A gamma source decreases from 6400 counts/min to 50 counts/min in 96 minutes. Calculate the half-life. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Count how many times you halve 6400 to reach 50: that is 7 times (6400→…→50). 7 half-lives fit in 96 min, so half-life = 96÷7 ≈ 13.7 min.

gold.display: An X-ray photon has a wavelength of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the frequency. Give your answer as a coefficient × 10¹⁸ (enter the coefficient, e.g. 3.0).

misconceptions.message: f = v÷λ. When dividing in standard form, subtract the exponent: 10⁸÷10⁻¹⁰ = 10¹⁸. f = 3.0×10¹⁸ Hz.

gold.display: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. A hospital needs it to have at least 25% of its original activity when it arrives. The transit time is 12 hours. Is the sample still usable on arrival?
options: Yes — 12 hours is 2 half-lives, leaving 25% of original activity
No — 12 hours is 3 half-lives, leaving only 12.5% of original activity
Yes — activity does not decrease significantly over 12 hours
No — any radioactive decay makes the sample unusable

misconceptions.message: n = 12÷6 = 2 half-lives. ½ × ½ = ¼ = 25% of original. Just meets the 25% threshold — the sample is borderline usable.
2 half-lives → activity × (½)² = ¼ = 25%. Exactly 25% remains, just meeting the minimum.
